Need latest (week 40/41).**Bottom line:** The latest FDOH report I found (Week 40, Oct 4–10) says **8 counties**. Brevard confirmed a local case on Oct 16 that isn't in that report yet, so the real floor is probably **9**. The question resolves on the Week 42 report, and the county count has kept growing all season.

**What the resolution sources say**
- I couldn't load the FDOH landing page directly, but I found its weekly PDFs and news coverage of them. The Week 40 report (Oct 4–10, 2026) says "368 cases of locally acquired dengue and 20 mosquito pools have been reported from eight counties".
- Cases by county as of Oct 10: Broward (1), Hillsborough (310), Miami-Dade (9), Orange (5), Palm Beach (1), Pasco (4), Pinellas (37), and Polk (1).
- The Metaculus FAQ link just defines which "credible sources" count if FDOH is unavailable. It doesn't affect the number.

**How the county count has grown (FDOH weekly reports)**
- Week 30 (Jul 26–Aug 1): 4 cases from three counties
- Week 32: 23 cases from four counties
- Week 33: 41 cases, four counties
- Week 34 (Pasco added): 73 cases… from five counties
- Week 35 (Orange added): 111 cases… from six counties
- Week 36: 152 cases… from six counties
- Polk was added around Weeks 37–38, making 7.
- Broward came next: on Oct 5, Broward confirmed its first local case of the year, the eighth Florida county with local transmission in 2026.
- Week 39 (Sep 27–Oct 3): 296 cases. Week 40: 368 cases, 8 counties.
- Overall, the count went from 3 to 8 counties in about 10 weeks, roughly one new county every two weeks. Case growth is still fast: 72 cases in Oct 4–10 alone.

**The newest development**
- On Oct 16, FDOH in Brevard County told residents about a confirmed human case of locally acquired dengue, its first. It wasn't in the Week 40 report, so the Week 41 report (Oct 11–17, likely out around Oct 22–23) will probably show 9 counties.
- Counties to watch for more spread: alerts are in effect for Hillsborough, Pinellas, Pasco, Miami-Dade, Orange, Duval and Alachua; advisories for Brevard, Broward, Holmes, Leon, Manatee, Martin, Palm Beach, Polk and Walton. Duval, Alachua and Manatee are under alerts or advisories but have no local cases yet.

**Base rates and context**
- 2026 is the largest outbreak in the US in decades; Florida's previous recent high was 199 cases in 2023.
- Earlier years' full-season county counts: 2023 had 186 cases in Broward, Hardee, Miami-Dade, Palm Beach, and Polk counties (5 counties). 2024 ended with 87 cases in 10 counties. In 2025, Florida reported 62 cases.
- Almost all transmission this year is DENV-2, traced to imported infections from Cuba, so new counties keep getting seeded by travel cases. Mosquito activity stays high into late October, and FDOH reports have lags.

**Timeline before resolution**
- The Week 41 report should come out around Oct 22–23.
- The Week 42 report (Oct 18–24) should come out around Oct 29–30, and that's the one that resolves the question.
- Counts are year-to-date cumulative, so they essentially never drop. One caveat: a county could be reclassified if a case's place of exposure is revised.

**Status quo:** If it resolved today on the latest published report, the answer would be **8**. Counting the Brevard case, it would be **9**. I didn't find any prediction-market prices for this question.

criterios: This question resolves to the number of counties stated in the "Dengue Cases Acquired in Florida" section of the Florida Department of Health (FDOH) weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report that is the most recent report published on or before October 30, 2026, available from the FDOH Arbovirus Surveillance page (https://www.floridahealth.gov/statistics-data/population-surveillance/arbovirus-surveillance/). That section states the 2026 year-to-date total in the form "In 2026, X cases of locally acquired dengue and Y mosquito pools have been reported from N counties." The question resolves to N, the number of counties. For example, if the report reads "...have been reported from nine counties," this resolves as 9.
letra_pequena: The relevant report is the single most recent weekly Florida Arbovirus Surveillance PDF dated on or before October 30, 2026 (expected to be the Week 42 report, covering October 18–24, 2026). If the FDOH page or PDF is temporarily unavailable, resolution waits until it is accessible or until the figure is reported by [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions). If the report omits the county count for locally acquired dengue but states the cumulative case total, the county count will be taken from the report's "2026 Mosquito-Borne Disease Activity by County" table (counting counties with at least one locally acquired dengue case). If FDOH permanently ceases publishing these reports and no equivalent county figure is available, the question is annulled.

(a) **Time left:** About 10–11 days until the report expected around October 29–30.

(b) **If nothing changed:** The latest published report would give **8 counties**. Brevard’s newly confirmed local case makes **9** likely in the next report.

(c) **If the recent trend continued:** Roughly one new county every two weeks points to **9–10 counties** in the resolving report.

(d) **Experts and markets:** I have no reliable expert forecast or prediction-market estimate for this specific county count.

(a) **Time left:** About 10–11 days. The resolving Week 42 report (Oct 18–24) should be published around Oct 29–30, 2026.

(b) **If nothing changed:** 8 counties, from the Week 40 report. Brevard's first local case, confirmed Oct 16, will almost certainly appear in Week 41. That makes 9 the practical status quo.

(c) **If the current trend continued:** The count has risen by about one county every two weeks (3 to 8 in roughly 10 weeks). Cases are still growing fast, with about 70 or more per week. Two more weekly reports after Week 40 imply about 10 counties. Brevard plus one more county is the central case, and possibly two more.

(d) **Experts and markets:** I found no markets. The question creator caps plausibility around 14. FDOH alerts and advisories cover additional counties without local cases yet (Duval, Alachua, Manatee, Martin, Leon and others). These are candidates for new local transmission, though some alerts are driven by travel cases.

(e) **Low-outcome scenario:** Reporting lags or a reclassified place of exposure keep Brevard out of the report. Cooling late-October weather also slows spread, so the count stays at 8 or 9.

(f) **High-outcome scenario:** Several counties with active alerts confirm local cases in the same window, for example Manatee, Duval, Alachua or Martin, near the large Hillsborough cluster. Delayed investigations clearing at once could push the count to 12–13.
